title: Jere D. Gallagher
text:
in memorium
Throughout her career, Dr. Jere Dee Gallagher was highly regarded and esteemed as an authority on child development. She dedicated most of her time to the University of Pittsburgh’s School of Education, where she eventually rose to the position of associate dean. During her tenure, she was instrumental in creating the Kinder Kinetics Program in the Health and Physical Activity Department, which she directed for over 25 years and considered her life’s crowning achievement

English and Portuguese interface.

title: Web app
text:
Privacy
Nothing is saved online or in your browser. Results disappear when you close or reload the page, so download the CSV first if you need it. That makes the Rater a good fit for teaching and practice: students can rate classmates or videos without creating accounts or storing children’s data.






This is a prototype for teaching and practice. For research data collection, follow the testing protocols and record forms on the Download page.



The earlier prototype (overhand throw only) is still online.

title: See how well a child moves, in two yes/no questions per skill.
text:
Movement skills assessment · Ages 5–10
      See how well a child moves, in two yes/no questions per skill.
      
        FG-COMPASS helps teachers, coaches, clinicians and researchers rate how children perform
        10 everyday movement skills, like throwing, kicking and jumping, on a simple 1–4 scale.
        You watch the child live. No video, no lengthy checklists.
      
      
        
           Download the decision trees
        
        
           Read the manual
        
      
      Free PDF · Research-validated · Built for schools, clinics and labs
    

    
    
      
        Try it
         Overhand throw
      
      Question 1 of 2
      Did the trunk rotate to the side of the throw during preparation?
      
        Yes
        No
      
      
        4
        
          Level 4 · Proficient
          
        
      
      
        
          1234
        
        
           Try again
        
      
    
  




  
    10movement skills
    2subtests: locomotor & object control
    5–10years of age
    4proficiency levels
    Liveobservation, no video needed
  




  
    
      Why it matters
      Movement skills are the building blocks of an active, healthy childhood.
    
    
      
        Running, jumping, throwing and catching are fundamental movement skills. Children who move well
        tend to be more physically active, and research links these skills to healthier body composition,
        stronger thinking skills such as working memory, and more confident play with peers.
      
      
        Spotting where a child is, and where they are stuck, lets you teach the next step and catch delays early.
        FG-COMPASS makes that check fast enough to do in a regular class or clinic session.
      
    
  




  
    How it works
    Watch, answer, score. That's it.
    
      
        
        Watch the child perform a skill
        Observe the skill live, in the gym, playground or clinic. A short protocol covers setup, instructions and trials for each skill.
      
      
        
        Answer two yes/no questions
        The first question points toward the lower or upper levels. A second question confirms where the child lands.
      
      
        
        Get a level from 1 to 4
        Record the level for each skill to see a child's profile, track progress or compare before and after a program.
      
    

    
      
        The decision tree in action
        Every skill uses the same three-question tree. Each child follows one path: a key question, then one confirming question.
      
      
        No
        Yes
        Yes
        No
        No
        Yes
        Question 1Key feature seen?
        Question 2Early patternconfirmed?
        Question 2Mature patternconfirmed?
        Level 1Initial
        Level 2Emerging
        Level 3Developing
        Level 4Proficient
      
      
         
         Pause
      
    

    
       For researchers: the composite decision-tree model
      
        
          
            FG-COMPASS is a process-oriented, criterion-referenced instrument. Each skill is scored with a
            composite decision tree that combines the Observational Plan and Three-Stage approaches to
            FMS assessment, using only three key performance criteria drawn from validated and hypothesized developmental sequences.
          
          
            Discriminatory question (DQ) separates the extremes (levels 1 and 4).
            Upper confirmatory question (UCQ) confirms level 4; if not confirmed, the child is level 3.
            Lower confirmatory question (LCQ) confirms level 1; if not confirmed, the child is level 2.
          
        
        
          
          Framework model shared by all ten decision trees.
        
      
    
  




  
    What it measures
    Ten skills, two subtests.
    
      
         Locomotor
        Moving the body from place to place.
        
          SkippingHoppingHorizontal jumpVertical jumpGalloping
        
      
      
         Object control
        Sending, receiving and controlling a ball.
        
          ThrowingCatchingKickingBattingStationary dribble
        
      
    
  




  
    Reading the results
    What the four levels mean
    Example: the overhand throw, from the first attempts to a mature throwing pattern.
    
      
        
        1Initial The key mature feature is missing and the early pattern is confirmed.Throw: the trunk faces the target and there is no step forward.
      
      
        
        2Emerging The key feature is still missing, but the child has moved past the early pattern.Throw: little or no trunk rotation, but the child steps forward.
      
      
        
        3Developing The key feature is present, but the mature pattern is not yet complete.Throw: the trunk rotates, with a short step on the opposite foot.
      
      
        
        4Proficient The key feature is present and the mature pattern is confirmed.Throw: the trunk rotates, with a long step on the opposite foot (at least half the child's height).
      
    
  




  
    Who it's for
    Practical enough for the gym, rigorous enough for the lab.
    
      
        
        PE teachers & coaches
        Check a whole class quickly, track progress over the year and see whether a program is working.
      
      
        
        Clinicians & therapists
        Spot movement delays early and plan targeted support, with clear levels to share with families.
      
      
        
        Researchers & students
        A process-oriented, criterion-referenced instrument with published reliability and expert-rater agreement.
      
    
  




  
    
      The evidence
      Built on more than 15 years of research.
      
        FG-COMPASS was developed at the University of Pittsburgh and tested for reliability and agreement with expert raters
        in peer-reviewed studies.
      
      See all publications 
    
    
      
        2024
        Expert-rater agreement and inter/intra-rater reliability of two locomotor skills
        Perceptual and Motor Skills
      
      
        2018
        Expert-rater agreement and inter-/intrarater reliability for FG-COMPASS
        Perceptual and Motor Skills
      
      
        2012
        The reliability of classification decisions for FG-COMPASS
        Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport
      
      
        2009
        Development and initial validation of FG-COMPASS
        Doctoral dissertation, University of Pittsburgh
      
    
  




  
    Get started
    
      
        
        Decision trees
        All 10 scoring trees in one PDF (v2.2).
      
      
        
        User manual
        Testing protocols, scoring and interpretation.
      
      
        
        Web app beta
        Rate all 10 skills on a phone or laptop. Nothing is stored.
      
    
    
      FG-COMPASS stands for the Furtado–Gallagher Children Observational Movement Pattern Assessment System
      (formerly the Furtado–Gallagher Computerized Observational Movement Pattern Assessment System).

title: Ovande Furtado JR
text:
Dr. Furtado received a B.A. in Physical Education from the Federal University of Parana, Curitiba, PR - Brazil. He earned his M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in Motor Behavior from the University of Pittsburgh, PA. Dr. Furtado’s line of research focuses on two main areas: (1) validation of observational models in psychomotor assessment instruments and (2) the relationship between motor skill competence, perceived motor competence, physical activity levels, and body composition.
